title: Beliefs & Foundations
description: General User → Mid. Familiar facts, broader basics and short everyday applications that build on Beginner knowledge of faith. Focuses on meanings and straightforward connections, without advanced theological debates or reference-number memorization. Scores reflect knowledge, not a judgment of faith.
levelMethod: Mid describes the knowledge and understanding required across all question styles. Styles are not difficulty levels. Requires more understanding and simple connections than Beginner, without specialist study. Editorial classification, not calibrated with learner response data.

review.referenceCheck: Linked Quran passages and hadith texts checked during preparation. Questions and explanations are original educational paraphrases, not verbatim translations. Everyday scenarios apply the cited principles. This is not independent scholarly approval.

selectionHints.unknownResponse: Use I am not sure as a separate UI action, not a fifth option.

questions.question: What does tawhid mean for a Muslim's worship?

options.text: Directing worship to Allah alone
Worshipping Allah and other beings together
Honoring every powerful being through worship
Treating all objects of worship as equal

questions.explanation: Tawhid includes worshipping Allah alone, the central call of His messengers.

questions.question: What purpose for humans and jinn is stated in the Quran?

options.text: To become independent of Allah
To worship Allah
To seek wealth as life's only goal
To avoid every responsibility

questions.explanation: The Quran identifies worship of Allah as the purpose of human and jinn creation.

questions.question: Which description expresses ihsan in worship?

options.text: Worshipping carefully only when people watch
Judging worship solely by its public appearance
Worshipping with awareness that Allah sees you
Assuming worship matters only in a mosque

questions.explanation: In the hadith of Jibril, ihsan involves worship with deep awareness of Allah's sight.

questions.question: What is shirk in the context of worship?

options.text: Learning about Allah's creation
Asking someone for ordinary practical help
Respecting one's parents
Associating partners with Allah

questions.explanation: The Quran identifies associating partners with Allah as a grave sin. Ordinary human assistance is not itself worship.

questions.question: What does the Quran teach about Allah's relationship to His creation?

options.text: Nothing is comparable to Him
He is simply the strongest created being
He depends on creation for knowledge
His nature can be measured like a creature's

questions.explanation: Allah is unlike His creation; the verse also affirms His hearing and sight.

questions.question: Which belief reflects Surah al-Ikhlas?

options.text: Allah needs others to sustain Him
Allah is needed by all and depends on none
Allah has a parent who created Him
Allah has an equal who shares His divinity

questions.explanation: The surah teaches Allah's oneness, independence and uniqueness.

questions.question: What duty of noble recording angels is mentioned in the Quran?

options.text: Deciding independently what Allah must know
Creating people's choices
Recording what people do
Choosing which humans deserve worship

questions.explanation: The Quran describes noble recording angels who know what people do.

questions.question: How are the angels mentioned in this verse described in relation to Allah's commands?

options.text: They decide which divine commands to reject
They require human worship to obey
They compete with Allah for authority
They obey what Allah commands

questions.explanation: The verse describes angels who do not disobey Allah and carry out His commands.

questions.question: According to the Quran, Iblis was one of which creation?

options.text: The jinn
The human prophets
The divine beings
The recording angels

questions.explanation: The Quran explicitly identifies Iblis as one of the jinn.

questions.question: To which prophet was the Zabur given?

options.text: Musa (Moses)
Dawud (David)
Isa (Jesus)
Yusuf (Joseph)

questions.explanation: The Quran names Dawud as the prophet given the Zabur.

questions.question: To which prophet was the Injil originally given?

options.text: Nuh (Noah)
Dawud (David)
Isa (Jesus)
Yunus (Jonah)

questions.explanation: The Quran states that Allah gave Isa the Injil as guidance and light.

questions.question: What does belief in Allah's messengers require?

options.text: Accepting only messengers from one's own people
Rejecting earlier messengers because Muhammad came later
Treating messengers as gods
Accepting all of His true messengers

questions.explanation: Muslims affirm all of Allah's messengers rather than accepting some and denying others.

questions.question: What does Muhammad being the final prophet mean?

options.text: No new prophet will come after him
Every later religious teacher becomes a prophet
His message has already been replaced
He was the only prophet ever sent

questions.explanation: The Quran calls Muhammad the seal of the prophets; Muslims believe prophethood concludes with him.

questions.question: How does the Quran describe Prophet Muhammad in relation to humanity and revelation?

options.text: A divine being who needs no revelation
A human messenger receiving revelation
An angel pretending to be human
A person whose message came only from his own opinions

questions.explanation: The Prophet is human and honored with revelation; worship belongs to Allah alone.

questions.question: What argument does the Quran give for Allah's power to restore life?

options.text: Life can return only if people remember every bone
Resurrection depends on worldly wealth
The One who created life first can restore it
Only those whose bodies remain intact can rise

questions.explanation: The Quran points to the first creation as evidence of Allah's power to resurrect.

questions.question: Who has knowledge of the exact time of the Last Hour?

options.text: Any person who studies enough calendars
Every religious teacher
Anyone who reports a vivid dream
Allah

questions.explanation: The Quran places knowledge of the Hour's appointed time with Allah.

questions.question: What does belief in qadar affirm?

options.text: Nothing happens outside Allah's decree
Events exist beyond Allah's knowledge and authority
Human planning guarantees every outcome
People can control the unseen by guessing

questions.explanation: The Quran teaches that Allah created everything according to a decree and measure.

questions.question: Which belongs to the articles of faith rather than the list of five pillars of Islam?

options.text: Fasting Ramadan
Belief in the angels
Paying zakah
Performing Hajj when able

questions.explanation: The hadith distinguishes the six articles of faith from the five pillars of Islam while teaching both together.

questions.question: How is the Quran described in relation to earlier scripture?

options.text: Rejecting the idea that Allah ever revealed books before
Being only a record of one tribe's customs
Confirming earlier revelation and serving as a criterion over it
Having no role in guidance

questions.explanation: The Quran confirms earlier revelation and serves as an authoritative standard over it.

questions.question: What does personal accountability mean in the Quran?

options.text: A person's family automatically bears every sin they commit
A famous name removes individual responsibility
Wealth allows a person to transfer all blame
No one carries another person's burden of sin

questions.explanation: Each person is accountable for their own deeds; family status does not transfer guilt.

questions.question: Does trusting Allah mean abandoning reasonable effort?

options.text: No, effort and reliance on Allah belong together
Yes, planning always shows weak faith
Yes, useful action contradicts belief in qadar
Only outcomes, never effort, deserve attention

questions.explanation: The Quran links decision-making with reliance on Allah, and hadith encourages pursuing benefit and seeking His help.

questions.question: Does belief in qadar remove responsibility for our choices?

options.text: Yes, wrongdoing never needs repentance
No, people remain responsible for their actions
Yes, every choice is automatically approved
Only other people's choices matter

questions.explanation: Belief in Allah's decree does not erase the Quran's teaching about human response and accountability.

questions.question: Does hardship by itself prove that Allah has rejected a person?

options.text: Yes, every difficulty proves rejection
Yes, believers are promised a life without loss
No, hardship can be a test
Only wealth can show that faith is accepted

questions.explanation: The Quran tells believers they will face tests involving fear, hunger and loss.

questions.question: Is worldly wealth alone a reliable measure of a person's honor before Allah?

options.text: Yes, the richest person is always the most righteous
Yes, poverty always means Allah despises someone
Only a person's public lifestyle matters
No, prosperity and restricted provision can both be tests

questions.explanation: These verses challenge treating wealth as automatic honor or limited provision as automatic humiliation.

questions.question: What attitude toward past sins does the Quran encourage?

options.text: Hope in Allah's mercy and a sincere return to Him
Despair that makes repentance pointless
Confidence that continuing every sin needs no concern
Assuming only people without a past can repent

questions.explanation: Allah calls sinners not to despair of His mercy; that hope invites returning to Him.

questions.question: What kind of repentance does the Quran call for?

options.text: An apology intended only to impress people
Sincere repentance
A performance with no wish to change
Blaming everyone else while defending the wrong

questions.explanation: Repentance should be a sincere turning back to Allah, not an empty outward display.

questions.question: Does Allah know deeds that remain hidden from other people?

options.text: No, only public deeds are known
Only if someone records them on a device
Yes, His knowledge includes the hidden and the apparent
Only if the person announces them

questions.explanation: The Quran describes Allah's complete knowledge, including things concealed from us.

questions.question: Can a person independently possess Allah's complete knowledge of the unseen?

options.text: Yes, if they become popular enough
Yes, if they charge for predictions
Yes, if their guesses sometimes come true
No, complete knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah

questions.explanation: People do not independently share Allah's all-encompassing knowledge of the unseen.

questions.question: What do the verses about an atom's weight of deeds teach?

options.text: Even small good and evil deeds matter
Only famous deeds are accountable
Small harms never matter
Only deeds witnessed by many people count

questions.explanation: The Quran emphasizes the significance of even very small deeds in accountability.

questions.question: Why can two outwardly similar good deeds differ in reward?

options.text: The more expensive clothing always earns more
The intentions behind them can differ
The deed with more photographs must be better
Only the person's age determines the reward

questions.explanation: The hadith teaches the importance of intention; outward resemblance does not tell the whole story.

questions.question: When claiming a specific act as prescribed worship, what matters beyond good intentions?

options.text: How fashionable the act becomes
Whether it is difficult to perform
A sound basis in the religion's guidance
How many people post about it

questions.explanation: The Prophet warned against introducing into the religion what does not belong to it. A specific claim about worship needs a sound basis.

questions.question: Can admiration for a prophet justify worshipping that prophet?

options.text: Yes, admiration always makes worship appropriate
Yes, if the prophet is widely loved
Only if the person also gives charity
No, prophets are honored while worship belongs to Allah alone

questions.explanation: Respect for Allah's messengers must remain consistent with worshipping Allah alone.

questions.question: How should angels be understood in relation to Allah?

options.text: Honored servants, not divine partners
Equal gods who share His rule
Beings who deserve worship because they are unseen
Sources of authority independent of Allah

questions.explanation: The Quran describes them as honored servants who act according to Allah's command.

questions.question: What fundamental call was shared by Allah's messengers?

options.text: Make every messenger a separate god
Worship Allah and reject false objects of worship
Accept only the customs of one modern nation
Seek wealth regardless of right and wrong

questions.explanation: The Quran describes the common call to worship Allah and turn away from false worship.

questions.question: Which response reflects both parts of the shahadah?

options.text: Honor Muhammad while rejecting Allah's oneness
Affirm Allah's oneness but deny His messenger
Worship Allah alone and accept Muhammad as His messenger
Treat Muhammad as a partner in divinity

questions.explanation: The testimony affirms Allah's sole right to worship and Muhammad's messengership.

questions.question: What does Allah's nearness in the verse about dua encourage?

options.text: Assuming He cannot hear ordinary people
Believing only famous people may ask Him
Waiting until one knows every religious rule before asking
Turning to Him in supplication

questions.explanation: Allah invites His servants to call on Him and respond to His guidance.

questions.question: Which response to revelation is modeled by the believers in this verse?

options.text: Listening, obeying and seeking forgiveness
Treating guidance only as decoration
Demanding praise before following guidance
Assuming belief removes every need to obey

questions.explanation: The verse joins belief with obedience, seeking forgiveness and awareness of return to Allah.

questions.question: What does the Quran teach about our judgment of what benefits us?

options.text: Everything we dislike must be harmful
Our preferences do not give us complete knowledge
Everything we desire must be good
Our immediate opinion is always wiser than revelation

questions.explanation: The verse reminds us that Allah knows while our knowledge is limited.

questions.question: Does feeling sadness or shedding tears necessarily contradict faith?

options.text: Yes, a believer can never feel sorrow
Yes, every tear is rejection of Allah's decree
No, grief can coexist with faith and patient speech
Only people with no faith experience loss

questions.explanation: The Prophet wept at his son's death while speaking in a way pleasing to Allah.

questions.question: What does the Quran teach about Allah's judgment on the Last Day?

options.text: A famous family name automatically decides every judgment
Small deeds are always ignored
Human popularity is the final standard
No person will be treated unjustly

questions.explanation: The Quran describes just scales and affirms that no soul will be wronged.

questions.question: You can do a task honestly or cheat while no one is watching. Which thought reflects ihsan?

options.text: Allah sees me even when other people do not
Only what people notice has moral importance
Hidden actions cannot affect my accountability
Being alone removes every duty

questions.explanation: Awareness of Allah encourages integrity beyond public appearances.

questions.question: You are preparing for an important exam. Which approach best reflects tawakkul?

options.text: Skip preparation to prove reliance
Prepare carefully, seek Allah's help and entrust the outcome to Him
Assume studying guarantees the exact result you want
Refuse advice because planning shows weak faith

questions.explanation: Responsible preparation and reliance on Allah can be practiced together.

questions.question: A plan fails despite reasonable effort. Which response best fits the hadith?

options.text: Give up all useful effort forever
Insist the past must change because you are upset
Accept Allah's decree and continue pursuing what benefits you
Treat the failure as proof that every future effort is pointless

questions.explanation: The hadith combines useful effort, seeking Allah's help and accepting what has already occurred.

questions.question: You knowingly wronged someone and say, 'It was decreed, so I owe no apology.' What is the better understanding?

options.text: The statement removes all responsibility
The victim now carries your sin
Believing in qadar makes every action lawful
Qadar does not excuse the wrong; repent and address the harm

questions.explanation: Allah's decree is not an excuse to avoid repentance or responsibility for harming someone.

questions.question: A friend says past sins make returning to Allah pointless. What response reflects the Quran?

options.text: Encourage sincere repentance and hope in Allah's mercy
Agree that worship can never matter again
Tell them only a perfect past allows repentance
Urge them to continue because change is impossible

questions.explanation: The Quran's call not to despair supports a sincere return to Allah.

questions.question: Someone wants to repent but plans to continue the same wrong without concern. What needs to change?

options.text: Only the wording of the announcement matters
Repentance should include a sincere desire to turn away from the wrong
More people need to watch the apology
The wrong becomes harmless if it is renamed

questions.explanation: Sincere repentance is more than declaring words while intending to defend the wrongdoing.

questions.question: You can quietly help someone in a small way. What belief encourages you to do so?

options.text: Only large public projects count
An unnoticed kindness has no value
Even small good deeds matter to Allah
Good deeds matter only if photographed

questions.explanation: Accountability includes small deeds, so a modest act of good should not be dismissed.

questions.question: You returned something honestly and nobody noticed. Which belief remains relevant?

options.text: The deed is unknown to Allah until someone reports it
The deed cannot matter without public thanks
Only recorded video can establish that it happened
Allah's knowledge is not limited to what people observe

questions.explanation: Allah knows actions regardless of whether other people see or praise them.

questions.question: An online account claims independent, certain knowledge of everyone's future. How should you assess that claim?

options.text: Reject the claim that this account possesses such knowledge
Accept it if the account has many followers
Accept it if the predictions are expensive
Treat dramatic presentation as proof

questions.explanation: Popularity, payment and confident delivery do not grant a person Allah's knowledge of the unseen.

questions.question: A video announces the exact date of the Last Hour. Which response follows the Quran?

options.text: Accept it if the video is widely shared
Do not accept the claim; its exact timing is known to Allah
Use the date to abandon all responsibilities
Assume a detailed calculation guarantees certainty

questions.explanation: The Quran does not give people authority to set the Hour's date.

questions.question: A practicing Muslim faces a painful loss. Which conclusion should you avoid?

options.text: Believers can face trials
Patience can matter during hardship
The loss proves Allah has rejected them
Support may be needed during difficulty

questions.explanation: Hardship alone does not establish someone's standing before Allah; believers are also tested.

questions.question: Someone calls a wealthy person automatically more beloved to Allah than a poor person. What is the better response?

options.text: Income alone settles the matter
Poverty always proves divine rejection
Expensive possessions guarantee accepted worship
Wealth alone does not establish spiritual rank

questions.explanation: The Quran corrects simplistic judgments based on abundance or restriction of wealth.

questions.question: You learn about a prophet from a people different from yours. What does faith require?

options.text: Respect and belief in every true messenger of Allah
Rejecting him because he is from another people
Accepting only prophets with familiar names
Treating nationality as the test of prophethood

questions.explanation: Belief in Allah's messengers crosses ethnic and national boundaries.

questions.question: A new teacher claims to be a prophet after Muhammad. Which belief applies?

options.text: A teacher's popularity creates prophethood
Muhammad is the final prophet
A claim is true whenever it sounds inspiring
Every generation must appoint a prophet

questions.explanation: The finality of Muhammad's prophethood rules out new prophetic claimants after him.

questions.question: You are about to help at a community event. Which intention should you cultivate?

options.text: Making everyone feel inferior to you
Earning praise regardless of how people are treated
Seeking Allah's pleasure through useful service
Proving that no other volunteer matters

questions.explanation: Sincerity gives direction to outwardly good work and guards against showing off.

questions.question: A post promises a guaranteed religious reward for a newly prescribed ritual without evidence. What should you do?

options.text: Assume detailed instructions prove it is prescribed
Accept it because the reward sounds attractive
Add it to the religion because it is popular
Check the religious basis with reliable sources or a qualified teacher

questions.explanation: Specific claims about prescribed worship and rewards need evidence, not just enthusiasm.

questions.question: You feel too ordinary to ask Allah for help. What does the verse about dua encourage?

options.text: Call upon Allah; His invitation includes His servants
Wait until you become famous
Assume only religious leaders can be heard
Avoid dua until you know every scholarly term

questions.explanation: Dua is not reserved for prominent people; Allah invites His servants to turn to Him.

questions.question: An outcome disappoints you even though you hoped for it. Which thought reflects humility about knowledge?

options.text: My immediate preference proves what must be best
I do not know every consequence, while Allah knows
Every disappointment proves all effort is useless
My limited view is the final measure of wisdom

questions.explanation: Our knowledge of outcomes is limited. Recognizing this can accompany continued responsible effort.

questions.question: Someone claims a respected family background removes responsibility for wrongdoing. What principle applies?

options.text: Family reputation transfers every sin elsewhere
An ancestor's status cancels personal duties
Each person is accountable for their own deeds
Only people from unknown families face judgment

questions.explanation: Honor associated with a family does not remove personal accountability.

questions.question: A grieving believer cries after a death. Which response reflects the Prophet's example?

options.text: Accuse them of rejecting Allah merely because they cry
Demand that grief end immediately
Tell them faith means never feeling sadness
Offer compassion; tears can coexist with faith

questions.explanation: The Prophet's tears show that natural grief need not contradict patience or faith.
